categoryDescription: User must be able to easily identify content using their senses: sight, sound, and touch.
title: Low contrast
description: Geometries and large text must have >3:1 contrast against background, Regular text must have >4.5:1.

goodExampleUrl.title: High contrast for data visualization with examples – Observable
goodExampleUrl.text: This interactive notebook demonstrates how to achieve high contrast in data visualisations. It explains that regular text should have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 and non‑text elements (like chart geometries) need a 3:1 contrast. Examples show how to measure contrast using colour pickers and dropper tools to ensure charts are accessible for viewers with low vision.

url.title: WebAIM Contrast Checker
url.text: The WebAIM Contrast Checker lets designers enter foreground and background colours to calculate contrast ratios. It reports the ratio and shows whether the combination meets WCAG AA or AAA criteria, helping people adjust colours so that text and UI elements have sufficient contrast:contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}.

url.title: Understanding Non‑Text Contrast – WCAG 2.1
url.text: WCAG 2.1’s non‑text contrast guideline requires that user‑interface components and graphical objects (such as icons, form controls and charts) have a contrast ratio of at least 3 :1 against adjacent colours. Maintaining sufficient contrast helps people with low vision distinguish important elements.

notes: Low contrast is the most common failure (88% of audits we have performed fail this). It also has the potential to be one of the most inclusive design spaces for representing data, perhaps outside of text treatment, content, and narrative design. Myndex Research (APCA/SPCA work) has noted the limitations of the WCAG 2.0/2.1 Model (which is based off of IEC/4WD 61966-2-1). The WCAG 3.0 Standard is likely to be much better, but work is still ongoing and not likely to become standard until at least 2025 or later.

categoryDescription: User must be able to easily identify content using their senses: sight, sound, and touch.
title: Content is only visual
description: Information in the chart must be available without visuals (no screen reader/braille support). At a minimum test using JAWS + Chrome, NVDA + Firefox (on Windows), VoiceOver + Safari (on Mac), and VoiceOver + Safari (on iOS). These devices must be able to access all chart information. All annotations, “visually apparent” trends or features, and all major narrative elements must be exposed to screen readers. Videos, presentations, and animations must include synchronized audio descriptions.

goodExampleUrl.title: Accessible Chart Demonstration (video)
goodExampleUrl.text: This video demonstrates an accessible chart with keyboard navigation and audio description. It shows how all chart information, annotations and trends are exposed to screen readers so that visually impaired users can understand the data without relying on the visual presentation.

url.title: VoiceOver User Guide for Mac – Apple Support
url.text: Apple’s VoiceOver guide explains how to use the built‑in screen reader on macOS. It includes instructions for enabling VoiceOver, navigating with keyboard shortcuts or a braille display and customising voices, helping blind and low‑vision users interact with apps and websites.

url.title: NV Access – Home of the free NVDA screen reader
url.text: NV Access is a non‑profit organisation that develops NVDA, a free open‑source screen reader for Windows. The home page explains that many of the world’s 285 million visually impaired people cannot afford commercial screen readers, so NVDA provides speech output and braille support at no cost:contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}.

url.title: JAWS Screen Reader – Freedom Scientific
url.text: The JAWS product page describes a widely used Windows screen reader that provides speech and braille output. It lists features such as optical character recognition to read inaccessible text, multiple synthesiser options and keyboard commands to navigate documents, web pages and applications:contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}.

url.title: Use TalkBack screen reader on Android – Google Accessibility
url.text: Google’s support page explains how to turn on and use TalkBack, the built‑in screen reader on Android devices. It covers enabling TalkBack in settings, using gestures and keyboard shortcuts to explore by touch and configuring speech feedback, helping users who are blind or low‑vision to operate their phones.

url.title: WCAG Quick Reference – Text Alternatives
url.text: The WCAG quick reference summarises requirements for text alternatives. It states that non‑text content, such as images or charts, must have text descriptions so that information can be presented in alternative modalities like screen readers or braille.

notes: The heart of this test is about non-visual access via text alternatives and generally, screen readers and braille readers (in the tools section of this test) are "assistive technologies" (AT) that can determine if this has been done accessibly. Broadly the considerations here in this test may need to expand beyond just using these AT devices someday, depending on whatever technologies are used by people.

categoryDescription: User must be able to easily identify content using their senses: sight, sound, and touch.
title: Small text size
description: Text (any) must not be smaller than 9pt/12px in size. Ideally only minor text is rendered at 9pt (Eg. axis labels) while all other text is larger.

url.title: Effects of small text on legibility (Vision Research)
url.text: This research article examines how small print sizes affect reading speed and legibility. It found that text smaller than about 9 pt (roughly 12 px on screens) significantly reduces readability, supporting recommendations that chart labels and annotations use at least 9 pt text.

notes: Testing for font size is highly complex and difficult if it isn't stored in data/metadata or known by the designer/developer. This is a difficult metric to measure and more tooling is needed to help with this. In addition, WCAG 2.1 has no requirement for text size. Ongoing work for 3.0 (thanks to Myndex) is integrating contrast evaluation with "size" (roughly approximating perceptial angle), since plenty of research has shown that size affects discriminability. But as we mentioned in the contrast limitations, this work is ongoing and non-standard. For more community resources, see: https://accessibility.psu.edu/fontsizehtml/

categoryDescription: User must be able to easily identify content using their senses: sight, sound, and touch.
title: Visual presents seizure risk
description: Chart must not pose a seizure risk when static or active. Chart must avoid red flashes and should avoid animating with red or have a significant portion of the display area use the color red. Tools like PEAT may be used to assess risk.

url.title: Photosensitive Epilepsy Analysis Tool (PEAT) User Guide
url.text: This user guide from the University of Maryland’s TRACE Research & Development Center introduces PEAT, a tool that analyses video and multimedia content to detect flashes and patterns that may trigger seizures. It explains how to use the software to scan media for red flashes and rapid flicker and interpret results to minimise seizure risk.

url.title: Understanding Three Flashes or Below Threshold – WCAG 2.0
url.text: The WCAG understanding document for the seizure guideline explains that content should not contain flashes that exceed three per second or red flashes that could trigger seizures. Designers should avoid flickering visuals and high‑contrast patterns to protect users with photosensitive epilepsy:contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}.

notes: We also acknowledge the work of South et al in their IEEE VIS poster where they used interaction techniques already built into three interactive visualizations to produce sequences capable of inducing seizures. We believe that the complex nature of interactive data experiences could merit more methodological attention for evaluating seizure risk.

categoryDescription: User must be able to easily identify content using their senses: sight, sound, and touch.
title: Color is used alone to communicate meaning
description: Color must not be the only channel for conveying meaningful or essential information. For categorical color schemes: Textures, shapes, or size (for filled elements) or dash patterns (for lines and paths) are required.

goodExampleUrl.title: No use of colour alone in data visualization – Observable
goodExampleUrl.text: This notebook illustrates why colour should not be the only channel for conveying information in charts. It shows examples of scatterplots where categories are encoded using both colour and textures or shapes, demonstrating that adding patterns makes charts accessible to people with colour vision deficiencies.

url.title: Understanding Use of Colour – WCAG 2.1
url.text: The WCAG guideline on colour use states that colour alone must not convey information, prompt responses or indicate status. Designers should use shapes, patterns, text labels or other visual cues in addition to colour so that people who cannot perceive colour differences can still understand the content:contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}.

notes: While this standard is very difficult for the field of data visualization to wrestle with, there is also little research that explores effective strategies. We need more work in this space, especially for color schemes that scale based on numerical data (sequential, ordinal, etc). See: https://observablehq.com/@frankelavsky/experimental-color-scale-textures

categoryDescription: User must be able to easily identify content using their senses: sight, sound, and touch.
title: Meaningful elements can be distinguished from each other
description: Primary chart elements must not be obscured by other elements (only a failure if discriminability or separability is required to understand the chart). Adjacent elements must have at least 1px white space between them (like stacked bars or pie charts where elements “touch”). Text (any) must not be obscured or overlapped by any other elements.

goodExampleUrl.title: Contrast and no use of colour alone in scatterplots – Observable
goodExampleUrl.text: This section of an Observable notebook demonstrates techniques for making scatterplots accessible. It shows how to ensure sufficient contrast between adjacent elements, add white space between overlapping marks and use shapes or textures instead of relying solely on colour.

url.title: Understanding Distinguishable – WCAG 2.1
url.text: The ‘Distinguishable’ guideline within WCAG explains that text and visuals should be presented so that users can separate foreground from background. It includes requirements for contrast, non‑text contrast and colour use to ensure important content is perceivable:contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}.

notes: Distinguishability is the higher level principle (above contrast) and helps guide how contrast is calculated. But it also is generally concerned with how we "perceive one thing from another," which is why this is separate from contrast. The gestalt techniques here especially have a very different approach than with contrast.

categoryDescription: User must be able to easily identify content using their senses: sight, sound, and touch.
title: Not CVD-friendly
description: Color choice should be “colorblind safe” (distinguishable to people with color vision deficiencies). Use tools like Viz Palette or Chroma to test the chart's color palette. Must not have major warnings on either.

goodExampleUrl.title: How your colorblind and colorweak readers see your colors – Datawrapper Blog
goodExampleUrl.text: Datawrapper’s article explains how different types of colour vision deficiency affect perception. It notes that around 8 % of men of European descent have red–green deficiencies and shows how certain colour combinations are hard to distinguish. The article gives tips for designing charts that are readable for colour‑blind readers:contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7}:contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}.

url.title: Viz Palette – colour palette design tool
url.text: Viz Palette is an interactive tool for creating and previewing colour palettes for data visualisations. Users can pick and edit colours, view how palettes appear in bar charts or line charts and export palette values. The tool also checks for colour‑blind friendliness and displays lightness information:contentReference[oaicite:9]{index=9}:contentReference[oaicite:10]{index=10}.

url.title: Chroma.js Colour Palette Helper
url.text: The Chroma.js palette helper helps designers build sequential or diverging colour palettes. It allows specifying palette types, arranging input colours and checking lightness. The tool simulates colour vision deficiencies and provides CSS and JSON outputs for use in visualisations:contentReference[oaicite:11]{index=11}:contentReference[oaicite:12]{index=12}.

url.title: Developing heuristics for accessible statistical graphics (UX research)
url.text: This research paper proposes a methodology for evaluating accessibility of statistical graphics for people with low vision or colour vision deficiencies. Through literature review and validation studies, the authors develop heuristics covering contrast, labelling, interactivity and other factors to make charts more accessible:contentReference[oaicite:13]{index=13}.

notes: Obviously we would imagine that standards require color vision deficiency consideration and this is actually where "no use of color alone" comes from. However, while it is assumed that having both high contrast and textures can resolve all CVD issues, it is still important to test color schemes against CVD simulations. So this heuristic is considered based on research, which we use Martínez et al's heuristics research for CVD in charts here.

categoryDescription: User must be able to easily identify content using their senses: sight, sound, and touch.
title: Spacing is inappropriate
description: Use of white space and other forms of padded, structured spacing should be appropriate. Too much or too little white space on charts with intervals (like a bar chart with thin bars and large gaps or vice a versa) can cause perceivable and understandable issues.

goodExampleUrl.title: Data Visualisation Principles Part 1: White Space, Text and Colour
goodExampleUrl.text: This article explains that white space is not wasted space but a critical design element. It recommends balancing macro and micro white space to improve readability, using legible fonts (minimum 12 px) and choosing colour palettes carefully. Proper use of white space, text size and colour improves the clarity and aesthetics of charts.

url.title: Whitespace: Not Just A Waste of Space – Callia Web
url.text: Callia Web’s article argues that whitespace is a valuable design tool, not wasted space. It defines whitespace as the blank areas around content and explains that it improves readability, creates balance, and groups related items, guiding the viewer’s eye through the design:contentReference[oaicite:16]{index=16}:contentReference[oaicite:17]{index=17}.

notes: While Headings and Labels are standards (2.4.6 and 2.4.10) for spacing and hierarchy reasons, "white space" specifically is a lower-level consideration that is massively important in effective, accessible data visualization. There is a research gap in this space. Another community article: https://medium.com/nightingale/how-to-use-whitespace-the-punctuation-between-visual-elements-5ff449709759

categoryDescription: All controls must be error-tolerant, discoverable, and multi-modal (not just mouse operable, but using keyboard, etc).
title: Interaction modality only has one input type
description: If chart is interactive with a mouse (or another input device) it must also be made interactive for use with a keyboard. Test navigating to chart with keyboard, using tab and arrow keys. Focusing should mirror hovering, selecting (enter or spacebar) should mirror clicks. The chart must also be tested with a touch device and screen reader, as these devices may have different experiences than a keyboard.

goodExampleUrl.title: Progressive Access: Accessible Chemistry Diagrams
goodExampleUrl.text: The Progressive Access project provides interactive chemical diagrams that are accessible across devices. The site describes features such as keyboard and menu‑driven exploration, magnification, high‑contrast and different colour schemes. An automated conversion workflow generates accessible SVG diagrams that work with screen readers:contentReference[oaicite:18]{index=18}.

url.title: Understanding Keyboard (No Exception) – WCAG 2.1
url.text: This WCAG success criterion states that all functionality must be operable using a keyboard without requiring specific timings or multipoint gestures. It ensures that pointer‑based interactions have keyboard equivalents and that people who cannot use a mouse can still operate controls:contentReference[oaicite:19]{index=19}.

notes: The keyboard interface (not literal keyboards but the technology they use to interface with software) is the single, most important thing to build and ensure when creating interactive content. Screen reader operability should always be tested alongside keyboard-only testing. In addition, we also should consider touch interaction. But how do we think about touch interfaces? Touch input often follows what is called the "pointer" interface, coupling mouse and touch interactions together. But touch has a much larger hit area, causing significant accessibility issues on mobile devices. This is largely an unsolved problem.

categoryDescription: All controls must be error-tolerant, discoverable, and multi-modal (not just mouse operable, but using keyboard, etc).
title: No interaction cues or instructions
description: If chart has any interactive capabilities at all, it must be explained somewhere for users to understand. All keyboard controls must also be explained as well.

goodExampleUrl.title: SF COVID‑19 Data and Reports – Dashboard Accessibility Information
goodExampleUrl.text: San Francisco’s COVID‑19 data dashboard provides keyboard instructions for interactive charts. Users press Ctrl+Enter to enter the dashboard, use Tab or arrow keys to navigate between visuals, press Ctrl+→ to enter a chart or filter, and use Space or Enter to select options. These cues help keyboard and screen reader users interact with the data:contentReference[oaicite:20]{index=20}.

url.title: Understanding Labels or Instructions – WCAG 2.1
url.text: The WCAG page on labels and instructions explains that form fields and interactive controls must include visible labels or clear instructions. Providing succinct labels helps users, particularly those with cognitive disabilities, understand what information is required:contentReference[oaicite:21]{index=21}.

notes: We have had long battles (in professional experience) with designers on this point. "Why do I need to provide instructions? If it is a good design, no instructions are needed!" And that simply is an ableist assumption. Instructions must be provided for any and all interactivity, including instructions for different input devices: hovering with a mouse or navigating with a keyboard.

categoryDescription: All controls must be error-tolerant, discoverable, and multi-modal (not just mouse operable, but using keyboard, etc).
title: Controls override AT controls
description: Custom keyboard and touch controls must not override screen reader settings. Any custom key controls must only apply when the chart or elements have focus (no page or app overrides).

goodExampleUrl.title: SF COVID‑19 Data and Reports – Dashboard Accessibility Information
goodExampleUrl.text: San Francisco’s COVID‑19 data dashboard provides keyboard instructions for interactive charts. Users press Ctrl+Enter to enter the dashboard, use Tab or arrow keys to navigate between visuals, press Ctrl+→ to enter a chart or filter, and use Space or Enter to select options. These cues help keyboard and screen reader users interact with the data:contentReference[oaicite:22]{index=22}.

url.title: Character Key Shortcuts (SC 2.1.4) – WCAG 2.1
url.text: The WCAG specification for character key shortcuts requires that authors provide a way to turn off single‑character shortcuts, remap them to include non‑printable keys (such as Ctrl or Alt) or ensure they are only active when the target component has focus. This prevents conflicts with screen readers and other assistive technologies:contentReference[oaicite:23]{index=23}.

notes: Not only are "keyboard traps" one of the worst experiences for keyboard and screen reader users, but key control overrides (such as overriding the native functionality of the tab key) can cause users significant issues.

categoryDescription: All controls must be error-tolerant, discoverable, and multi-modal (not just mouse operable, but using keyboard, etc).
title: Low contrast on interactive elements
description: When interactive elements use color to communicate a change of state (like changing opacity, saturation, or hue on hover, focus, or selection), the new state should have at least 3:1 contrast against its previous state. Use WebAIM Contrast Tool or dropper tool. However, contrast color difference is not required if additional indications are provided, such as stroke thickness change (of at least 2px difference), a dash pattern is used, a marker is added, or other high-contrast technique. Ideally, both color and non-color strategies are used together (redundantly).

goodExampleUrl.title: Visa Chart Components – Utils: Interactivity
goodExampleUrl.text: The Visa Chart Components utils library includes functions for accessible interactivity. `setElementFocusHandler` adds focus listeners to highlight elements when navigating via keyboard; `setElementInteractionAccessState` toggles interactive elements to semantic buttons; and `setElementAccessID` assigns unique IDs to tie elements to ARIA properties. These utilities help developers create chart components that meet keyboard and screen reader requirements:contentReference[oaicite:24]{index=24}.

url.title: Understanding Non‑Text Contrast – WCAG 2.1
url.text: WCAG 2.1’s non‑text contrast guideline requires that user‑interface components and graphical objects (such as icons, form controls and charts) have a contrast ratio of at least 3 :1 against adjacent colours. Maintaining sufficient contrast helps people with low vision distinguish important elements.

notes: State change for interactivity is important to communicte clearly, arguably imperative for something to be operable. This is a good example of a strong intersection between Perceivable and Operable principles. We put this heuristic into operability primarily because while it is related to perceivability, it determines operability.

categoryDescription: All controls must be error-tolerant, discoverable, and multi-modal (not just mouse operable, but using keyboard, etc).
title: Keyboard focus indicator missing, obscured, or low contrast
description: Visual keyboard focus indication must be present and easy to see. Focus indicator must have 4.5:1 contrast against background, must not be fully obscured, and must have at least a 2px border. Use WebAIM Contrast Tool or dropper tool.

goodExampleUrl.title: Visa Chart Components – Utils: Interactivity
goodExampleUrl.text: The Visa Chart Components utils library includes functions for accessible interactivity. `setElementFocusHandler` adds focus listeners to highlight elements when navigating via keyboard; `setElementInteractionAccessState` toggles interactive elements to semantic buttons; and `setElementAccessID` assigns unique IDs to tie elements to ARIA properties. These utilities help developers create chart components that meet keyboard and screen reader requirements:contentReference[oaicite:26]{index=26}.

url.title: Understanding Focus Appearance (Minimum) – WCAG 2.2
url.text: The focus appearance criterion requires that keyboard focus indicators be large enough and contrast sufficiently with the unfocused state. Specifically, the focus indicator must cover an area at least as large as a 2 CSS‑pixel border around the element and have a contrast ratio of at least 3 :1, helping users locate the current focus:contentReference[oaicite:27]{index=27}.

notes: Focus indication is one of the most important and also least-designed parts of accessible visualizations. In all of our review, we only found custom, author-provided focus indication in Visa Chart Components and with some Apple charts, when leveraging their accessibility tree. All other keyboard-navigable charts appear to use default styles and assumptions (about enclosure, size, color, etc).

categoryDescription: All controls must be error-tolerant, discoverable, and multi-modal (not just mouse operable, but using keyboard, etc).
title: Inappropriate tab stops
description: Interactive elements (that represent buttons, links, or selectable features) must have a tab stop, while non-interactive elements must not have a tab stop. Every interactive chart element must NOT have its own tab stop unless the chart is small or the tabs are programmatically revealed (such as having a single tab stop at the root of a chart and then a way to enter further layers or sections of the chart using keyboard controls). At least one tab stop should be provided if a data table succeeds the chart and is interactive, otherwise a table should not have a tab stop.

goodExampleUrl.title: Chart Component Boilerplate – Observable
goodExampleUrl.text: This Observable notebook provides a template for building accessible chart components. It includes code examples showing how to implement keyboard navigation, set tab order, manage focus and apply ARIA attributes so that complex charts can be explored using a keyboard:contentReference[oaicite:28]{index=28}.

url.title: Understanding Focus Order – WCAG 2.1
url.text: WCAG’s focus order criterion requires that interactive elements receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability. Keyboard users should encounter content in a logical sequence, such as row‑by‑row or left‑to‑right, so that navigation is predictable:contentReference[oaicite:29]{index=29}.

notes: This failure is very common for chart design on the web. Often, tabindex will be given to every single element in a chart, even if those elements aren't interactive. This is bad! I believe this practice stems from difficulty making SVG-driven charts accessible to screen readers and keyboard users alike. Note that progressively disclosing layers of tabindexed elements is a good strategy, care should still be taken to avoid placing too much tedium on the user in cases where the chart's childmost layer is dense (see "Navigation is tedious" in Assistive.

categoryDescription: All controls must be error-tolerant, discoverable, and multi-modal (not just mouse operable, but using keyboard, etc).
title: Complex actions have no alternatives
description: Special actions (brushing/zooming/filtering/gesturing) that use custom or complex chart controls must have a standard UI alternative available. These controls must be clear and easy to use with a keyboard, screen reader, and touch device.

url.title: Understanding Multiple Ways – WCAG 2.1
url.text: The multiple ways criterion encourages providing at least two ways to locate content, such as through navigation menus, search functions or sitemaps. Offering alternative navigation methods helps users with disabilities find information more easily and reduces reliance on memory:contentReference[oaicite:30]{index=30}.

notes: Both standards for 2.4.5 "Multiple Ways," 2.5.4 "Motion Actuation," and 2.5.1 "Pointer Gestures" all engage this issue. All special actions must have alternatives. Good design even considers alternatives that are not 1 to 1 translations. A 1 to 1 translation might be making a chart keyboard navigable and interactive to match a mouse hover/click. Alternative design for "multiple ways" might be also to provide a search function across the data or chart space in order to directly select elements.

categoryDescription: All controls must be error-tolerant, discoverable, and multi-modal (not just mouse operable, but using keyboard, etc).
title: Target pointer interaction size is too small
description: Interactive elements that can be targeted by a mouse or touch pointer interaction should have a minimum size of at least 24px x 24px. If elements are scaled according to data values (such as a scatterplot or otherwise), then alternative means must be provided to select, activate, or otherwise interact with the information or task that the element represents.

goodExampleUrl.title: How the House Got Stuck at 435 Seats – FiveThirtyEight
goodExampleUrl.text: This interactive project examines how the U.S. House of Representatives has remained fixed at 435 seats since 1910. It uses visualizations and simulations to show how apportionment works, highlighting that population growth and fixed seats create inequities in representation and exploring proposals for expanding the House:contentReference[oaicite:31]{index=31}:contentReference[oaicite:32]{index=32}.

url.title: Understanding Target Size (Minimum) – WCAG 2.2
url.text: The target size criterion states that interactive elements activated via pointer input should be at least 24 × 24 CSS pixels. Alternatively, equivalent spacing or another control can be provided. This ensures controls are large enough for users with limited dexterity:contentReference[oaicite:33]{index=33}.

notes: This is quite a hard requirement for accessibility in visualization because the spatial dimensions of visual marks are often mapped to variables. We argue that alternatives should be provided such as text labels that satisfy minimum size, accompanying data tables or search functions, alternative navigation and input (such as with a keyboard or non-precise touch input), or features like zooming or filtering. While we applaud efforts such as the use of voronoi diagrams on top of visualizations, we believe that these still pose significant operability barriers for people with motor impairments.

categoryDescription: Any information or data are presented without ambiguity, with clarity, and in a way that minimizes cognitive load.
title: No explanation for purpose or for how to read
description: Chart should explain its purpose and how to read, use, and interpret it.

url.title: Beyond Memorability: Visualization Recognition and Recall
url.text: This study measured recognition and recall of 393 visualizations across 33 participants. The authors found that charts with descriptive titles and supporting text were more likely to be correctly recalled. Pictograms helped recognition when used judiciously, and redundant encoding (using multiple visual channels) improved communication:contentReference[oaicite:34]{index=34}.

notes: The criteria for 1.3.6 "Identify Purpose," 3.3.2 "Labels or Instructions," and 3.3.5 "Help" all fail to necessitate explaining how to read a complex data visualization. Even simple data visualizations can give people trouble interpreting or understanding.

categoryDescription: Any information or data are presented without ambiguity, with clarity, and in a way that minimizes cognitive load.
title: No title, summary, or caption
description: A title, summary, context, or caption must be provided.

url.title: Beyond Memorability: Visualization Recognition and Recall
url.text: Research into visualization recall shows that memorable graphics often include clear titles, labels and narratives. The study suggests that providing titles, summaries or captions helps viewers understand and remember what a chart conveys, highlighting the importance of descriptive text:contentReference[oaicite:35]{index=35}.

notes: We use Borkin et al here. The criterion 2.4.6 "Headings and Labels" is interesting in that it doesn't require headings and labels to be present, but only requires them to be sufficiently descriptive IF present. This is a serious flaw in the current standards, which is why we look to research in this space. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/headings-and-labels.html

categoryDescription: Any information or data are presented without ambiguity, with clarity, and in a way that minimizes cognitive load.
title: Reading level inappropriate
description: All text (and alternative text) provided must target a reading grade level of 9 or lower. Tools may be used to automate reading level estimation.

url.title: Hemingway Editor
url.text: The Hemingway Editor is an online tool that analyses text and highlights complex sentences, adverbs and passive voice. It assigns a readability grade level and suggests simpler alternatives, helping writers adjust their content to a ninth‑grade reading level or below.

url.title: Understanding Meaningful Supplements – WCAG 2.0
url.text: This WCAG understanding document explains that if complex or unfamiliar terms are used, authors should provide definitions or supplementary material. Simplifying language and defining jargon helps people with cognitive disabilities understand content.

notes: Special circumstances may require complex terminology, but these should be explained using a reading grade level of 9 or lower.

categoryDescription: Any information or data are presented without ambiguity, with clarity, and in a way that minimizes cognitive load.
title: Interactive context is not clear
description: If chart can affect the logic or layout of the page or if receives data or parameters from other UI controls or logic, this must be clearly communicated in text. Alerts or notifications must be provided that can be monitored programmatically without requiring navigation (to notify screen reader users, for example).

url.title: Understanding Status Messages – WCAG 2.1
url.text: The status messages guideline requires that important updates or changes in content be programmatically conveyed to assistive technologies. This allows screen readers to announce updates like form submission results or dynamic alerts without shifting focus, keeping users informed:contentReference[oaicite:36]{index=36}.

notes: Interactive charts often affect different areas of a page or view and different areas of a page or view can often affect charts. This relationship should always be clear to the user, as well as changes to state caused by the chart or its context. This uses criteria 4.1.3, 3.3.5, and 3.3.2.

categoryDescription: Any information or data are presented without ambiguity, with clarity, and in a way that minimizes cognitive load.
title: Information complexity is inappropriate
description: Information complexity must be appropriate to the task or goal of the visual. Often, this is an issue when charts have too many different kinds of information encoded (note that this isn't the same as density). Chart must not have more than one Y or X axis without first presenting two chart separately. Chart must not encode along a third spatial dimension (z axis) unless the data itself is 3D (spatial, modeling, etc). Chart should not contain more than 5 data categories.

url.title: Design Guidelines for Statistical Graphics (FCSM paper)
url.text: This Federal Committee on Statistical Methodology paper discusses cognitive limitations in interpreting graphs. It recommends limiting charts to about five data categories, avoiding dual axes and 3D graphics and presenting separate charts before combining them. These guidelines help prevent cognitive overload and improve comprehension.

notes: Note that 5 Categories comes from meta-study on effective working memory (See Table 9: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4591021/). Dual axis graphs in particular have been a contentious topic in visualization. We have encountered arguments in favor of using them when your audience are "trained experts." However, we are not sure how someone can evaluate their own audience's level of skill in a way that also ensures accessibility. We are also unsure of the benefits afforded this small group. But in any case, the point here is to exercise significant caution and to know that using dual axis graphs is inaccessible to a broad audience (and likely even expert audiences) as it is primarily an attentive, not pre-attentive, chart design.

categoryDescription: Any information or data are presented without ambiguity, with clarity, and in a way that minimizes cognitive load.
title: Changes are not easy to follow
description: Chart changes must be easy to follow. If a chart’s data change is meaningful, it must employ animations for object constancy (no faster than 250ms or longer than 2s). Changes to state must be announced to screen reader users.

url.title: Designing Animated Transitions for Data Visualisation
url.text: This book chapter argues that when charts update, animating the transition helps maintain object constancy. It suggests keeping animations between 250 ms and 2 s: shorter animations may be hard to follow, while longer ones may frustrate users. The authors also recommend announcing changes to screen reader users.

notes: Object constancy, as Bostock refers to it, is likely understudied in visualization research and certainly hasn't been interrogated from an accessibility perspective. Much more work needs to be done here. We synthesized three different sources to get our range between 250ms and 2seconds: WCAG guidance says a limit of 5 seconds for animations without controls, we found that 2 seconds was a more appropriate limit in our own industry user studies for the domain of visualization, and 250ms minimal limit is from a meta-study on visual fixation duration in older adults.

categoryDescription: Any information or data are presented without ambiguity, with clarity, and in a way that minimizes cognitive load.
title: Metrics and variables are undefined
description: Metrics or variables must not be misleading or undefined. Chart must not lie and data (and source) must be defined. Metadata, metrics, calculations, and variables must be defined.

goodExampleUrl.title: Effective Practices for Description of Science Content within Digital Talking Books
goodExampleUrl.text: This guideline from WGBH’s National Center for Accessible Media provides advice on describing scientific charts and diagrams in audio. It emphasises defining variables, units and metrics, summarising key trends and relationships and including data tables where appropriate to make complex visuals understandable to blind readers.

notes: This seems straightforward enough on the surface: define the variables you are using. Often larger articles will explain variables or metrics in the body text of nearby paragraphs, but it is important to bring this information as close to a chart or data interface as possible so that someone can have the information ready and convenient.

categoryDescription: Any information or data are presented without ambiguity, with clarity, and in a way that minimizes cognitive load.
title: Statistical uncertainty isn't clearly communicated
description: Statistical confidence/uncertainty must be clearly and unambiguously communicated. If any statistical confidence interval exists, it must use clear conventions and provide textual explanation.

goodExampleUrl.title: Communicating Statistical Uncertainty in Visualisations (CHI 2018)
goodExampleUrl.text: This research paper investigates methods for communicating statistical confidence and uncertainty in charts. It finds that clear conventions such as error bars, violin plots or gradient shading, combined with textual explanations, help viewers understand uncertainty and make better decisions.

url.title: Communicating Statistical Uncertainty in Visualisations (CHI 2018)
url.text: This research paper investigates methods for communicating statistical confidence and uncertainty in charts. It finds that clear conventions such as error bars, violin plots or gradient shading, combined with textual explanations, help viewers understand uncertainty and make better decisions.

notes: Hullman and Padilla are arguably both the giants of research in this space. Both of them have many papers in this space worth exploring for techniques and findings. The biggest limiation worth noting is that due to the complexity of this space, there may be contexts where it isn't entirely clear how to best communicate uncertainty (both from a cognitive accessibility standpoint and ethically).

categoryDescription: Any information or data are presented without ambiguity, with clarity, and in a way that minimizes cognitive load.
title: Axis labels are unclear or missing
description: Axis labels should be present and clear. Axis must not be truncated without a clear label. In rare cases axes may be removed (if adequate text explanation or annotation is provided). Otherwise, axis should be present and clearly labeled. Axis labels may be abbreviated but with a clear and consistent convention.

url.title: Chart Axis Best Practices – Yellowfin BI
url.text: Yellowfin’s guide recommends including axis titles and units, starting axes at zero when appropriate and using consistent intervals. It warns against truncating axes without clear labelling and emphasises that clear axis labels prevent misinterpretation of the data.

notes: We really could use some robust research into axis labelling and design. Not only are there plenty of annoying engineering concerns in this space, but the low-level nature of effective axis design makes it a somewhat tricky problem. The high-level concerns for axis design (not being misleading, when truncation is appropriate, etc) are also relatively understudied from a research perspective. I think that this particular test could easily become a set of standards in our field.

categoryDescription: Any information or data are presented without ambiguity, with clarity, and in a way that minimizes cognitive load.
title: Controls are inappropriate
description: All controls provided must not be irrelevant to the message, question, or task of the chart. Chart's interactive scope and functionality must not be too broad. The chart should if it can have irrelevant functionality removed.

url.title: Add Value – Inclusive Design Principles
url.text: The ‘Add Value’ principle advises designers to include only controls and features that add value to the user. Avoiding unnecessary options and complexity reduces cognitive load and ensures that interactive elements support the task at hand rather than distracting from it.

notes: This one is actually quite hard to find good example articles for because it seems so obvious. Clearly, one might think, we should not have controls and functionality that are effectively useless or excessively taxing to use. Every component, module, widget, and control we provide should add value. Despite this seeminly apparent requirement, in the our past auditing and industry work we have found that many cognitive barriers exist when interactive data visualization tools and applications have more controls than are necessary for the task. This seems like an easy paper or blog waiting to be written! (See: any dashboard in Tableau. They are all able to drag-select, click, and hover even when those interactive features provide virtually no value to the user. Tableau, especially has a problematic interaction-by-default approach.)

categoryDescription: The design is compliant with existing standards and works with the user’s compliant, assistive technologies of choice.
title: Does not conform to standards
description: The chart must conform to appropriate compliance standards. The chart must pass all relevant WCAG 2.1, Section 508, or equivalent requirements where applicable. (This is intended as an automatic failure until the chart can be fully evaluated.)

url.title: Understanding Ensure Compatible Parsing – WCAG 2.0
url.text: This WCAG understanding document explains that web content should use markup in a way that can be unambiguously parsed. Elements should be properly nested and have unique start and end tags so that assistive technologies can interpret content consistently and reliably.

notes: Chartability is not intended to compete against or completely replace any existing standards and guidelines but work alongside them.

categoryDescription: The design is compliant with existing standards and works with the user’s compliant, assistive technologies of choice.
title: Semantically invalid
description: Semantically invalid use of document elements (if it functions like a button, but it is semantically other than a button, etc). Chart must be semantically valid according to modern standards. Initial testing (on the web) may be automated using any combination of: Axe-core, Wave, HTML Codesniffer, Accessibility Insights, or W3C Markup Validation but may only pass once a screen reader test has also verified the experience (see: Perceivable Failures for screen reader info).

url.title: axe DevTools – Automated Accessibility Testing
url.text: Deque’s axe DevTools is a suite of browser extensions and integrations that automatically scan web pages for accessibility issues. It identifies problems such as missing labels, improper ARIA attributes and colour contrast failures and provides guidance for remediation.

url.title: Understanding Name, Role, Value – WCAG 2.1
url.text: The name, role and value criterion requires that user interface components have programmatically determinable names, roles and states. Custom controls must expose these properties so that assistive technologies can identify what the control is, what it does and its current state:contentReference[oaicite:37]{index=37}.

categoryDescription: The design is compliant with existing standards and works with the user’s compliant, assistive technologies of choice.
title: Fragile technology support
description: Chart access must not be isolated to one browser, device, software, or operating system. There must be a diversity of technological means to access the chart and its information and functionality.

url.title: Understanding Concurrent Input Mechanisms – WCAG 2.1
url.text: This guideline ensures that content does not restrict the user’s ability to switch between input modes. Users should be able to use a keyboard, mouse, touch screen or other input devices interchangeably; prohibiting specific inputs or requiring certain gestures can exclude some users:contentReference[oaicite:38]{index=38}.

categoryDescription: (Understandable, yet Robust): Information flows must provide transparency, tolerance, and consideration for different ways that users with assistive technologies and disabilities will prefer to consume different information.
title: No table
description: A table must be provided that contains a human-readable version of the data the chart is based on. This may be excluded if the chart title, summary, context, or annotations are sufficient at conveying all relevant information contained in the chart.

goodExampleUrl.title: Effective Practices for Description of Science Content within Digital Talking Books
goodExampleUrl.text: This guideline from WGBH’s National Center for Accessible Media provides advice on describing scientific charts and diagrams in audio. It emphasises defining variables, units and metrics, summarising key trends and relationships and including data tables where appropriate to make complex visuals understandable to blind readers.

url.title: Effective Practices for Description of Science Content within Digital Talking Books
url.text: This guideline from WGBH’s National Center for Accessible Media provides advice on describing scientific charts and diagrams in audio. It emphasises defining variables, units and metrics, summarising key trends and relationships and including data tables where appropriate to make complex visuals understandable to blind readers.

notes: Supplying a table is supported by empirical research via the Diagram Center/NCAM but has also largely been adopted by attempts by the community wishing to bypass Section 508 difficulties making a chart or graph accessible. Tables are often used to fully replace charts, argued as if they are equivalent experiences. Chartability does not take this design position (having a table doesn't mean everything else about a chart can pass). I've discussed in the past that tables are not enough, especially from an interactivity and navigation perspective because chart structures can represent relationships that are non-tabular. See: "Information cannot be navigated according to narrative or structure." The Design System for the US Government states that while a table might provide equivalent access to the data, "a data table does not provide an equivalent narrative to a visualization," which is an important distinction. See: https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/data-visualizations/

categoryDescription: (Understandable, yet Robust): Information flows must provide transparency, tolerance, and consideration for different ways that users with assistive technologies and disabilities will prefer to consume different information.
title: Information can only be reached through single process
description: There must be more than one process available to reach the same information. If chart is contained within or participates in complex user interface flows, such as transitions between views or states, interacting with filters, or moving between pages, there must be alternative paths to reach that same state (such as with search features, parallel UI controls, etc).

url.title: Understanding Multiple Ways – WCAG 2.1
url.text: The multiple ways criterion encourages providing at least two ways to locate content, such as through navigation menus, search functions or sitemaps. Offering alternative navigation methods helps users with disabilities find information more easily and reduces reliance on memory:contentReference[oaicite:39]{index=39}.

notes: We have found that many analytical dashboards and applications suffer from their greatest strength, which is the ability to perform deep and complex analysis. These deeply exploratory experiences must have multiple ways to produce the same information. Ultimately, this is an information architecture problem. We recommend reading "Your Information Architecture is an Accessibility Problem" by Sarah Barrett: https://medium.com/known-item/your-information-architecture-is-an-accessibility-problem-cd54ae917f8e

categoryDescription: (Understandable, yet Robust): Information flows must provide transparency, tolerance, and consideration for different ways that users with assistive technologies and disabilities will prefer to consume different information.
title: Location and history is unclear
description: Current location in a system is not easy to understand. Similar to “more than one process” and “easy to share and reproduce,” current view and state of visualization (in a complex environment like a dashboard or app) must provide the user with breadcrumbs to guide their path as well as the ability to save, reload, and navigate history.

url.title: Understanding Location – WCAG 2.1
url.text: The location criterion advises providing information about the user’s position within a set of pages, such as breadcrumbs or step indicators. Knowing where they are helps users navigate complex interfaces, especially those with cognitive impairments or using assistive technologies:contentReference[oaicite:40]{index=40}.

notes: Breadcrumbs, history, and the ability to save and load all participate in systems that are robust, forgivable, error-tolerant, and kind to the user. Coincidentally, they are also all more accessible for cognitive reasons, especially when these features are communicated.

categoryDescription: (Understandable, yet Robust): Information flows must provide transparency, tolerance, and consideration for different ways that users with assistive technologies and disabilities will prefer to consume different information.
title: Interactions are not forgivable
description: Interactions and operations must be forgivable. When the visualization is interactive or has the ability to perform a task, the user must be able to both undo or redo their actions.

url.title: Designing for Error Tolerance (Human Factors Research)
url.text: This human factors study discusses the importance of making interactive systems forgiving of mistakes. It recommends providing undo and redo features, confirmation prompts and ways to recover from errors, acknowledging that users will make mistakes and that interfaces should be designed to tolerate them.

notes: Error tolerance, error-tolerant design, and ideas like Norman's "To Err is Human" are relatively old and well studied. This finds its way into standards, but is unfortunately limited in scope. Interaction errors in data experiences can be quite complex. The criteria for 3.3.6 "Error Prevention (All)" technically only applies to data entry and text fields.

categoryDescription: (Understandable, yet Robust): Information flows must provide transparency, tolerance, and consideration for different ways that users with assistive technologies and disabilities will prefer to consume different information.
title: Information cannot be navigated according to narrative or structure
description: Chart must provide a way to be navigated according to its data or narrative structure. The title, description, annotations, and then lower level data structures should be navigable and in that order. Chart data that contains sub-grouping (like a stacked bar chart) or nesting (like a treemap or hierarchy) must provide keyboard navigation that can navigate between levels and/or laterally across levels (in a non-linear fashion). Keyboard navigation must be comparable to the data structure (including cases where the data structure is novel) as well as provide linear or tabular navigation (like in a table or list).

goodExampleUrl.title: Progressive Access: Accessible Chemistry Diagrams
goodExampleUrl.text: The Progressive Access project provides interactive chemical diagrams that are accessible across devices. The site describes features such as keyboard and menu‑driven exploration, magnification, high‑contrast and different colour schemes. An automated conversion workflow generates accessible SVG diagrams that work with screen readers:contentReference[oaicite:41]{index=41}.

url.title: Accessible Navigation for Hierarchical Data (CHI paper)
url.text: This CHI paper proposes methods for navigating charts according to data structure rather than linear order. It introduces keyboard and screen reader techniques for exploring hierarchies and nested data, enabling users to move between levels and across siblings in charts like treemaps and grouped bar charts.

notes: We use Sorge et al as well as his later work with Godfrey here: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-94277-3_92. The criteria for 2.4.3 "Focus Order," 2.4.5 "Multiple ways," and 1.3.1 "Info and Relationship" get very close, but don't quite satisfy this. Early community attempts to engage this problem are Leonie Watson's "Accessible SVG Line Graphs" and Doug Schepers' work.

categoryDescription: (Understandable, yet Robust): Information flows must provide transparency, tolerance, and consideration for different ways that users with assistive technologies and disabilities will prefer to consume different information.
title: Table/data is static
description: Provided table must at least be downloadable, filterable, or sortable.

url.title: Inclusive Components: Data Tables
url.text: The Inclusive Components article on data tables warns against using tables for layout and describes how to mark up data tables correctly. It suggests using <table> with <th> elements and scope attributes so that screen readers announce row and column headers and recommends making tables sortable or downloadable for flexibility:contentReference[oaicite:42]{index=42}:contentReference[oaicite:43]{index=43}.

notes: This particular community recommendation actually comes from the our experience working with people with disabilities who are also data experts. In many cases, having a table that is downloadable as a CSV satisfies many concerns since programs like Excel actually handle a lot of needs. A CSV is a low-level, flexible material compared to a chart, meaning that it has more potential to be molded by the user into the experience that suits their needs. Despite this, it is preferable to make tables that are rendered filterable (ideally with a search feature) and sortable.

categoryDescription: (Understandable, yet Robust): Information flows must provide transparency, tolerance, and consideration for different ways that users with assistive technologies and disabilities will prefer to consume different information.
title: State is not easy to share and reproduce
description: Chart state must be easy to share and reproduce. If an analysis or complex interaction can produce a customized view, this view must be easy to share (such as with a single link, file, or saved state).

goodExampleUrl.title: Everything You Never Wanted to Know About Google Maps Parameters – Moz Blog
goodExampleUrl.text: Moz’s blog post explains the query parameters used in Google Maps URLs. By adjusting values such as latitude, longitude, zoom level and map type, users can create links that recreate the same map view, making it easier to share a specific location or state with others.

url.title: How to Share Power BI Reports – Key2 Consulting
url.text: This article describes several methods for sharing Power BI reports. It explains features like sharing through the Power BI Service, embedding reports into websites, publishing to the web and exporting to PDF, enabling collaborators to view interactive dashboards in the same state.

notes: Believe it or not, many complex dashboards and applications with a branching narrative or exploratory style of data interaction have no easy way to share their current state. In professional work in the past, we have found that this is a significant access barrier when an analyst digs deep into their analysis, discovers something worth sharing, and then has no easy way of sharing it. The resulting access barrier is often placed on others. It is both significant cognitive effort as well as a usability problem. Often, an analyst has to result to using a screenshot, but then the labor and "proof in the system" of the analysis is lost! In addition, screenshots are their own accessibility risk (as they must now be made accessible). We challenge engineers to consider how incredible google maps is at maintaining a user's exact parameters in a url so that if they share a link, whoever views it sees the same thing they do. The same cognitive-labor accessibility applies to other complex data interaction spaces.

categoryDescription: (Understandable and Perceivable but labor-reducing): Interface must be intelligent and multi-sensory in a way that reduces the cognitive and functional labor required for use.
title: Data density is inappropriate
description: Data must be presented at an appropriate density. If too many elements are competing for the same space (approximate limit is based on cognitive load): clustering or patterns (or lack of) must be explained, chart must be aggregated to a higher level with less elements, or chart must be divided into smaller charts with less data. Visual density should serve a purpose, such as retaining the data's signal (when appropriate).

goodExampleUrl.title: Stop Aggregating Away the Signal in Your Data – Stack Overflow Blog
goodExampleUrl.text: The Stack Overflow blog post argues that excessive data aggregation can hide important patterns. It advocates breaking data into comparable groups, adding meaningful categories and using both aggregate and granular views so that the underlying signal isn’t lost.

url.title: Bin‑Summarize‑Smooth: A Framework for Visualizing Large Datasets
url.text: Hadley Wickham’s paper proposes summarising large datasets by binning data into grids, computing summary statistics for each bin and smoothing to reduce visual noise. The technique aligns data to the display’s pixel grid and uses smoothing to mitigate artefacts, enabling responsive and interactive visualisations:contentReference[oaicite:45]{index=45}:contentReference[oaicite:46]{index=46}.

notes: Data density and comprehension might have studies? However, we couldn't find any research on this from a cognitive or perceptual perspective. Is that because this is such an "obvious" thing that nobody feels the need to question it? It is possible our lit review missed where these papers live.

categoryDescription: (Understandable and Perceivable but labor-reducing): Interface must be intelligent and multi-sensory in a way that reduces the cognitive and functional labor required for use.
title: Navigation and interaction is tedious
description: Large blocks of repeated content must be skippable and interactions where the user is required to perform significant labor must not be considered essential (in content or function). The number of interactions or time required to perform a single task should be measured and compared across modalities (mouse pointer versus sequential keyboard versus search versus voice, etc).

url.title: Understanding Bypass Blocks – WCAG 2.1
url.text: The bypass blocks criterion requires mechanisms like ‘skip to content’ links or headings that allow keyboard users to skip repetitive content. Providing ways to jump past long navigation menus or repeated headers improves efficiency for people using screen readers and keyboard navigation:contentReference[oaicite:47]{index=47}.

notes: Generally, the number of interactions or time required to complete a task is a usability measurement. But when different assistive technologies and inclusive design patterns are considered, this becomes an accessibility measurement as well. There should not be an access gap for someone's time investment in a data experience solely based on interaction and navigation means. There are significant cognitive accessibility overlaps as working memory and cognitive load increases throughout long and tedious interaction patterns.

categoryDescription: (Understandable and Perceivable but labor-reducing): Interface must be intelligent and multi-sensory in a way that reduces the cognitive and functional labor required for use.
title: Visually apparent features and relationships are not described
description: Trends, clusters, patterns, outliers, or significant statistical semantics and findings that are considered “visually apparent” must be described through text at a minimum. Optionally, these features may also be exposed using sonification or tactile means or through other multi-sensory approaches.

goodExampleUrl.title: Highcharts Accessibility: Sonification
goodExampleUrl.text: Highcharts’ accessibility documentation describes a sonification module that turns chart data into audio. Developers can map data values to pitch, duration or timbre and provide keyboard controls to play the chart, giving blind or low‑vision users a way to perceive trends and outliers using sound.

url.title: Understanding Info and Relationships – WCAG 2.1
url.text: This guideline emphasises that structural information conveyed visually must also be programmatically determinable. Proper use of headings, lists, table markup and ARIA landmarks allows screen readers to understand relationships and navigate content effectively:contentReference[oaicite:48]{index=48}.

notes: This heuristic is actually a significantly unsolved problem when it comes to the building materials we have available to us. Not only are sonifications or tactile experiences often authored in parallel (but separate) from visualizations (and tend to be a 1 to 1 representation), but we lack the semantic tools to describe relationships between parts (such as outliers, comparisons, trends, etc). Many efforts have attempted to automate textual descriptions, but as Lundgard et al point out, this may not be possible at a meaningful level we require in order to understand higher levels of information (see: "Accessible Visualization via Natural Language Descriptions"). This issue is related to 1.3.3 "Sensory Characteristics," but also 1.3.1 "Info and Relationships," which Brennan Young engages in a conversation on ARIA's github: https://github.com/w3c/aria/issues/991#issuecomment-668493619

categoryDescription: (Understandable and Perceivable but labor-reducing): Interface must be intelligent and multi-sensory in a way that reduces the cognitive and functional labor required for use.
title: Data in text is not human-readable
description: Data must be formatted to be human-readable. All textual information displayed (in data labels, annotations, axes, tables, legends, etc) must be formatted to an understandable level of content (ie “human readable”). These formats must also be made into versions that can be read and parsed comfortably by screen readers. (For example: 6500000000 should be formatted to 6.5b visually and to “six point five billion” when used in screen reader labels and alt text.)

url.title: Understanding Unusual Words – WCAG 2.1
url.text: The unusual words criterion advises authors to provide definitions or explanations for jargon, idioms and acronyms. Offering definitions or allowing users to look up unfamiliar terms helps people with cognitive disabilities and those using screen readers understand the content:contentReference[oaicite:49]{index=49}.

notes: It is strange that axis labels (especially) have not had an intelligent solution built yet that can parse all the possible states of axis-related data and turn them into something usable and well-formatted for human reading. This could even have implications for well-written alt-text. We believe that this could be a low-hanging fruit for researchers or builders to explore who are looking to make a tool or library that is helpful for many others.

categoryDescription: (Understandable and Perceivable but labor-reducing): Interface must be intelligent and multi-sensory in a way that reduces the cognitive and functional labor required for use.
title: Space does not handle extremes
description: Use of space should appropriately handle extreme difference or similarity in the data. Both extreme quantitative differences and similarities can produce unreadable charts. If chart elements are squished into margins due to outliers or together by too much similarity, this fails. Chart must automatically handle these issues or else it must be made clear to the user through annotations what is happening. If data is dynamic or producing automatic annotations is not possible, then chart must provide a way for the user to sort, divide, or filter the chart space on their own.

goodExampleUrl.title: Data Visualisation Principles Part 1: White Space, Text and Colour
goodExampleUrl.text: This article explains that white space is not wasted space but a critical design element. It recommends balancing macro and micro white space to improve readability, using legible fonts (minimum 12 px) and choosing colour palettes carefully. Proper use of white space, text size and colour improves the clarity and aesthetics of charts.

notes: Real data is often horrible. In analytical environments, especially those where a chart format is chosen and expected to display data that is the result of a user's interaction with parameters and filters, this problem becomes common. Charts must be adaptive and flexible to the extrema in the data (grow or change to fit new parameters) but also should recognize when parameters result in data that completes for the same space (mentioned in another heuristic). If two lines are so close together that it is almost impossible to see the difference between them, a new chart type might need to be chosen or some filtering should take place instead.

categoryDescription: (Understandable and Perceivable but labor-reducing): Interface must be intelligent and multi-sensory in a way that reduces the cognitive and functional labor required for use.
title: No default "build-your-own" provided
description: If the user is required to craft their own chart (say by combining variables in an analytic environment), a default, opinionated view of the data should be provided as a starting point.
notes: This particular example comes from our experience working with people with disabilities in product and application testing contexts. "Build your own" analytical experiences are really difficult from a cognitive perspective, especially if this intersects with other access needs.

categoryDescription: (Perceivable and Operable, yet Robust): Design must respect user settings from user agents (browsers, operating systems, applications) and provide presentation and operation control.
title: User style change not respected
description: Styling changed by the user must be respected. Chart must not interfere with or override styling changes made by the user (such as importing a custom style sheet for use in an HTML application or web site).

categoryDescription: (Perceivable and Operable, yet Robust): Design must respect user settings from user agents (browsers, operating systems, applications) and provide presentation and operation control.
title: Long animations cannot be controlled
description: Longer, video-style or explanatory animations must have pause, stop, and start controls. Specifically, animations lasting more than 2 seconds or any looping animations must be able to be paused or stopped. Animations used to communicate transitions in the state of the data that last more than 2 seconds must provide a way for the user to start over.

url.title: Give Control – Inclusive Design Principles
url.text: The ‘Give Control’ principle recommends giving users the ability to pause, stop or adjust long‑running animations and to turn off features like infinite scrolling. Allowing users to control how content changes makes experiences more accessible and reduces motion sickness and cognitive load.

categoryDescription: (Perceivable and Operable, yet Robust): Design must respect user settings from user agents (browsers, operating systems, applications) and provide presentation and operation control.
title: Scrolling experiences cannot be altered
description: Scrolling experiences must provide a way to be adjusted or opted out of. Infinite scrolling, parallax scrolling, and “scrollytelling” experiences must come with the ability to be turned off or used optionally, with an option like “load more” or “next” in its place for keyboard only users.

url.title: Give Control – Inclusive Design Principles
url.text: The ‘Give Control’ principle recommends giving users the ability to pause, stop or adjust long‑running animations and to turn off features like infinite scrolling. Allowing users to control how content changes makes experiences more accessible and reduces motion sickness and cognitive load.

categoryDescription: (Perceivable and Operable, yet Robust): Design must respect user settings from user agents (browsers, operating systems, applications) and provide presentation and operation control.
title: Zoom and reflow are not supported
description: Chart space must be able to be zoomed using assistive technology or equivalent. Text, geometries, and all elements must change size appropriate to the type of zoom used. When zooming, content should reflow and not be cut off from view in two directions. Responsive design may need to consider re-arranging the display to ensure that no meaningful information or functionality is lost during reflow.

url.title: Understanding Reflow – WCAG 2.1
url.text: The reflow criterion requires that content can be presented without loss of information or functionality when zoomed or viewed at a width of 320 CSS pixels. Pages should avoid horizontal scrolling and use responsive design so that text, images and controls wrap or stack appropriately:contentReference[oaicite:52]{index=52}:contentReference[oaicite:53]{index=53}.

categoryDescription: (Perceivable and Operable, yet Robust): Design must respect user settings from user agents (browsers, operating systems, applications) and provide presentation and operation control.
title: User's text adjustments are not respected
description: Text spacing and font-size changed by the user must be respected. Chart must not interfere with programmatic changes to font sizes or text spacing, such as importing a custom style sheet or using a browser’s build in zoom function. Font size and spacing must adjust accordingly.

url.title: Understanding Resize Text – WCAG 2.1
url.text: This guideline states that text should be resizable up to 200 % without assistive technology and without loss of content or functionality. Designers should use relative units and avoid preventing users from scaling text so that people with low vision can enlarge text for readability:contentReference[oaicite:54]{index=54}.

categoryDescription: (Perceivable and Operable, yet Robust): Design must respect user settings from user agents (browsers, operating systems, applications) and provide presentation and operation control.
title: Design is not consistent and familiar
description: Design must be consistent and familiar by default. Charts must be made consistent with one another across an application or environment, including sharing default styling and settings as well as those set by the user. Interaction defaults (such as keybindings or interaction patterns) should carry over between charts that perform the same task or funciton.

url.title: Understanding Consistent Identification – WCAG 2.1
url.text: The consistent identification criterion requires that components with the same function are labelled consistently across a site. Using consistent icons, labels and positions helps users recognise controls and reduces confusion, particularly for people with cognitive or memory impairments.

categoryDescription: (Perceivable and Operable, yet Robust): Design must respect user settings from user agents (browsers, operating systems, applications) and provide presentation and operation control.
title: Contrast and textures cannot be adjusted
description: Contrast or textures must provide a way to be adjusted as-needed. Chart must not interfere with or override user’s independent contrast adjustments and chart must adjust accordingly to new settings. Chart textures (such as those used on fills) must be able to be turned on or off according to user preference.

url.title: Experimental Colour Scale Textures – Observable
url.text: This notebook experiments with combining colour scales and textures. It introduces a library of textures that can be applied to colours to encode categories or values and simulates how these textures perform for colour‑blind users. The examples show how adjusting texture density and pattern can improve chart accessibility.

notes: In experiences with audiences in the past, we have found that if some chart textures are on by default, we are creating accessibility barriers due to their visual complexity (we lose or complicate pre-attentive features as well). So we argue that textures (whether on by default or not) must be able to be toggled according to user preference. Much more work and research needs to be done in this space, especially as it challenges the idea that a single design can satisfy everyone's access needs.

categoryDescription: (Perceivable and Operable, yet Robust): Design must respect user settings from user agents (browsers, operating systems, applications) and provide presentation and operation control.
title: Difficult chart type has no alternative
description: The user should be able to adjust the type or presentation of difficult or complex charts into more accessible alternatives that still accomplish the same analytical task.

goodExampleUrl.title: State of the States IDD Demo – CU VisualAB
goodExampleUrl.text: The IDD demo presents an accessible financial dataset about support services for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. It applies guidelines such as avoiding pie charts, limiting the number of categories and using discrete marks or isotype pictograms in bar charts and scatterplots. url.title: Accessible Visualisation for People with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities
url.text: This research paper explores the design of data visualisation tools for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD). It proposes alternative chart types such as treemaps with pictograms and simplified scatterplots, and suggests allowing users to switch between visual representations to match their cognitive needs.

notes: Pie charts, line charts without discrete marks, and bar charts without countable isotypes all pose cognitive difficultes. Chart types that are high risk for difficulty or misinterpretation should be presented alongside alternative charts or alternative explanations and charts should be available to help the user perform the same tasks. Optionally, users should be provided control over the presentation style of these chart types (eg change pies into treemaps or stacked bars, add discrete marks to line intervals, or add countable isotypes to divide bars).
